title: How Telescopes Work
objective: After this level you can tell refracting from reflecting telescopes and explain why bigger mirrors see more.
summary: Refractors use lenses, reflectors use mirrors. A bigger aperture gathers more light, so the largest telescopes are reflectors.

cards.headline: A telescope is a light bucket. Bigger bucket, more universe.
cards.body: Catching light is the whole game. The more a telescope catches, the fainter the things it can show you. So how do you build a better bucket?

cards.headline: Lenses or mirrors
cards.body: There are two ways to catch starlight. Refracting telescopes gather it with lenses. Reflecting telescopes gather it with a curved mirror. Isaac Newton built the first practical reflector in 1668, yes, the same Newton who later explained gravity. A lens you look through, or a mirror you look into: every telescope you'll meet picks one.

cards.headline: Why size matters
cards.body: Think of a bucket in the rain: the wider the opening, the more it catches. A wider mirror or lens collects more light, so it can see fainter objects and show finer detail. That's why astronomers keep building bigger. And the giants are all reflectors, because a huge lens sags under its own weight, while a mirror can be supported from behind. Big lenses droop. Big mirrors get a backrest.

cards.fact: The biggest optical telescopes today have mirrors about 10 meters across.
cards.context: Mirrors that size are often built from many smaller segments fitted together, like floor tiles. And the next buckets are already under construction, with mirrors more than 30 meters wide. That's more than three times as wide as today's biggest.

cards.headline: Telescopes: understood
learned: Refractors use lenses; reflectors use mirrors
Newton built the first practical reflector in 1668
Bigger apertures see fainter and finer

questions.prompt: What does a reflecting telescope use to gather light?

options.label: A radio antenna
options.rationale: Radio telescopes are a different kind.

questions.explanation: Reflecting telescopes gather light with curved mirrors; refractors use lenses.

questions.prompt: Why are the world’s largest telescopes all reflectors?

options.label: Mirrors show more colors than lenses
Newton banned large lenses
options.rationale: He built a reflector; he didn’t ban lenses.

options.label: Huge lenses sag, but mirrors can be supported from behind
Mirrors are cheaper to carry into space
options.rationale: Most large telescopes are on the ground.

questions.explanation: A giant lens can only be held at its edge and sags under its own weight. A mirror can be supported across its whole back.

questions.prompt: From Level 25: Galileo turned his telescopes to the sky in 1609. Why could later, bigger telescopes see much fainter objects?

options.label: They used brighter lenses
options.rationale: Lenses don’t add light; they collect it.

options.label: They were built on taller mountains only
options.rationale: Height helps a little; size matters most.

options.label: They magnified the stars more
options.rationale: Stars stay points of light even when magnified.

options.label: Their larger mirrors or lenses collect more light

questions.explanation: A wider mirror or lens collects more light, so bigger telescopes reveal fainter objects.
